title: Binary Search
summary: Halve the search range at every step, whether you are looking through a sorted array or through a range of possible answers.
keyPoints: Binary search needs a range where one side is definitely wrong and the other may contain the answer.
Use a half-open range [low, high) or a closed range [low, high], and keep the same convention throughout.
Compute the midpoint without overflowing in fixed-width languages.
The same pattern can search for a threshold answer, not just an index.

complexity.operation: Binary search on an answer range

commonMistakes: Using the wrong loop condition or returning the wrong endpoint for a half-open range.
Computing `(low + high) / 2` when the sum can overflow a fixed-width integer.
Forgetting that a rotated sorted array still has one sorted half at every midpoint.
Binary-searching when the data is not actually sorted or monotonic.
interviewNotes: Write down the invariant before the loop: what is guaranteed about everything left of low and right of high?
For a lower-bound search, decide whether equal elements should stop the search or continue left.
When the search space is numeric, explain how a candidate answer can be checked in O(n).

checkYourself.question: Why does binary search take O(log n) steps?
checkYourself.answer: Each step throws away about half of the remaining range. After k steps at most n / 2^k items remain, so about log₂(n) steps are enough.

checkYourself.question: In a rotated sorted array, how do you decide which half is sorted?
checkYourself.answer: Compare nums[low] with nums[mid]. If nums[low] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted; otherwise the right half is sorted. Then check whether the target falls inside that sorted half.

checkYourself.question: What does a lower-bound search return when the target appears several times?
checkYourself.answer: The index of the first occurrence, or the insertion point if the target is absent.
